release_channels.ask: How does the app reach people: app stores, a desktop installer, enterprise distribution? Are there beta channels?

supported_versions.ask: How long must older versions keep working once a new one ships?
supported_versions.why: Installed apps stay on people's devices, so the server has to keep talking to old versions.

rollout_plan.ask: How are releases rolled out and, if something goes wrong, rolled back?

store_review.ask: Which app stores' rules and review steps apply, and how long does a review usually take?
store_review.why: A release reaches people only once the store approves it, so a fix takes days rather than minutes, and store rules (payments, privacy labels, account deletion) shape features.
store_review.applies_when: The app is distributed through an app store.

forced_update.ask: When an old version can no longer work with the services, how are people moved off it: a prompt to update, a required update, or a switch on the server?
forced_update.why: Without a way to require an update, every old version must be supported for as long as anyone still has it installed.
forced_update.applies_when: The app is installed on phones, tablets or computers, rather than used only in a browser.

client_platforms.ask: Where does the app run: web browsers, iPhone and iPad, Android, desktop? Which comes first, and is each built separately or from shared code?
client_platforms.why: The platforms decide the client architecture, what can be shared, how it is released and what it is tested on.

device_permissions.ask: Which device features need the person's permission (camera, location, photos, contacts, notifications), and what does the app do when they say no?
device_permissions.why: The operating system asks the person, stores reject apps that ask without a clear reason, and every refusal needs a working fallback.
device_permissions.applies_when: The app is installed on phones, tablets or computers, rather than used only in a browser.

push_notifications.ask: Does the app send push notifications? What triggers each one, and can people choose which they get?
push_notifications.explain: A push notification is a message the operating system shows even when the app is closed, delivered through Apple's or Google's notification service.
push_notifications.applies_when: The app is installed on phones, tablets or computers, or uses browser notifications.

device_matrix.ask: Which devices, operating-system versions and screen sizes must the app work on, and which of them are tested before each release?
device_matrix.why: Installed apps run on hardware nobody on the team controls. The list sets what 'works' means and what the end-to-end checks run on.
device_matrix.applies_when: The app is installed on phones, tablets or computers, rather than used only in a browser.

user_created_data.ask: What do users create or change in the app, and what happens to it when they leave?
user_created_data.why: Data people create is the heart of an application's state model.

offline_use.ask: Must the app work without an internet connection? If so, what happens when changes made offline conflict?
offline_use.why: Offline support changes how data is stored, synced and recovered. If the answer is no, the offline parts of the design can be skipped.
offline_use.explain: Syncing is copying changes between the device and the server once a connection returns.

empty_error_states.ask: What should users see on first use, when there's nothing to show yet, and when an action fails?

docs/application/RELEASES.md.purpose: How installed client versions are released, supported, rolled out and rolled back.
docs/application/RELEASES.md.skip: Created only when the app ships as an installed client.
